💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass.
  • At home in London, he highlights me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

Recent findings suggest that this is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

At home in London, he highlights me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he says. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”.

In a recent development, ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he states.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”.

“It’s not physically hard with significant weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”.

“What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, at the moment. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”.

Industry observers note that “I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”.

Sources indicate that “10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”.

Sources indicate that “From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”.

It has been revealed that “I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”.

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”.

It has been revealed that “I’m big on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”.

Industry observers note that “I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”.

According to recent reports, “I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”.

According to recent reports, “I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”.

It has been revealed that “Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”.

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone said the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”.

Recent findings suggest that “No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”.

#180645. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1152 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Upcoming York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she indicates. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

In a recent development, but while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, claims that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she claims. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Tech Report: A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do.
  • Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery.
  • The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a significant, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Off-White x Nike Air Max 97 ‘White’.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

It has been revealed that arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

Air Jordan 1 High OG ‘Yin Yang’.

In a recent development, the Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

Sources indicate that we’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

A version of the story originally appeared on British GQ.

#180638. As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1688 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release.
  • Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child.
  • I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first newly introduced installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, swiftly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

By the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

Industry observers note that the third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a new city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between new installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that reveals videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

After several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It says so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that departing GOP Rep.
  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, stated Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

Recent findings suggest that departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

Industry observers note that there’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the upcoming Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

In a recent development, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Recent findings suggest that absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

According to recent reports, “The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy stated in a Friday statement.

#180630. This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November.
  • In a recent development, zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market.
  • Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

In a recent development, zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that fresh business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta said. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”.

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy said. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all promptly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

When it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the upcoming onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also released this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

That watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta said they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us new clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”.

Recent findings suggest that zenith created irresistible bait for this newly introduced stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

Industry observers note that the dials of the new collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

In a recent development, zenith looks to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

With the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are currently booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

  • “I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” says Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Fresh York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” claims Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in Newly introduced York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. unveiled that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” says Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Fresh York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” claims Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in Newly introduced York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”.

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

Sources indicate that in skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” claims Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

Recent findings suggest that the world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” indicates Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

“The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” says Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”.

Carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson says. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

As for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” says Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”.

Instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she states. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Industry observers note that peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” indicates Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson indicates.

And, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson indicates. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”.

‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer.
  • After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.
  • It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

According to recent reports, though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I stated, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Industry observers note that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

According to recent reports, also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy noted Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he mentioned, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In a recent development, in the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

Recent findings suggest that but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, mentioned she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

Sources indicate that and several Senate GOP aides mentioned that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the looks and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Recent findings suggest that republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott mentioned. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

Recent findings suggest that an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

In a recent development, sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

In a recent development, one senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

In a recent development, cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he noted, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

Exclusive: Shohei Ohtani Just Signed a Historic Deal With New Balance

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that shohei Ohtani is used to making history.
  • In a recent development, now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner Upcoming Balance through to the end of his baseball career.
  • It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the Upcoming England sportswear stalwart for the long haul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

In a recent development, now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner Upcoming Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.).

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the Upcoming England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”.

Sources indicate that earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at Newly introduced Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance rolled out in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

According to recent reports, while conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

“I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani states. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a massive change. They understand what I want.”.

Ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, Newly introduced Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”.

While some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”.

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” says Masahiro Uchida, New Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”.

At 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his Latest Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

According to recent reports, ohtani still looks on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”.

It has been revealed that what words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

It has been revealed that expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

It has been revealed that to get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”.

Sources indicate that inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

Latest Congress will still be filled with losers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct.
  • OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.
  • Sources indicate that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

Sources indicate that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

It has been revealed that “We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown revealed his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” stated a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

It has been revealed that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Latest Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Credit for inventing crêpes Suzette is claimed by French restaurateur Henri Charpentier, who in 1894, at age 14, while an assistant waiter, accidentally set a sauce aflame when serving dessert to the Prince of Wales. Once the fire subsided, the sauce was so delicious that the prince asked that the dish be named for a young girl in his entourage, Suzette.

Featured in “Blazin' Pancakes” by Mindy Fox in the January/February 2000 concern and  “Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?” by Ellery Weil.

According to recent reports, outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that with the space aglow in Ferrari Rosso Scuderia red under a shiny mirrored disco ball and a checkered-flag DJ booth, guests snacked on wagyu bites and gourmet caviar-topped chicken nuggets and sipped on-theme cocktails. (Also served: SkinCeuticals’s top-shelf favorites, including the P-TIOX and C E Ferulic serums, passed around on silver trays.) The model Kelly Piquet, partner of F1 star Max Verstappen, posted up on the green velvet banquette, as other attendees played around with SkinCeuticals-branded poker chips and cards around the room.

In a recent development, on the venue’s outdoor terrace overlooking the glowing marvel that is Sphere, actor Chace Crawford and his dad, dermatologist Chris Wayne Crawford, took a moment to enjoy the view. The two were doing a little father-son bonding—a perfect setting since F1 is “a male, testosterone-fueled sport,” joked Chris. As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” remarked the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

Sources indicate that inside, sportscaster and former Seattle Seahawk superstar Russell Wilson, a big F1 fan, couldn’t wait for lights-out-and-away-we-go on Sunday. He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he stated, “so I’m fired up about it.”.

Recent findings suggest that at 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. When the musician Sooin, of the K-pop group Meovv, hopped into the booth to chop it up with the Chainsmokers, the room lit up.

They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.

“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”.

Chace Crawford and Chris Wayne Crawford.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

According to recent reports, whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

It has been revealed that toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

According to recent reports, heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.
